title: Amazon Redshift out-of-the-box performance innovations for data lake queries
key_points: Explains why missing statistics hurt lake queries and what Redshift now does without them: distributed dynamic partition elimination, cached Iceberg metadata, and estimates of column width from Iceberg manifests.
Collecting Puffin statistics on Iceberg tables still gives the planner more to work with.
AWS reports roughly 2x faster TPC-DS 3 TB runs on Iceberg without statistics between the late-2023 and mid-2025 releases; the Nov 2025 post covers later scan-layer gains, so read the two together.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3
decision: Load lake data into Redshift managed storage vs query Iceberg/Parquet in place (with or without collected statistics)
authors: Martin Milenkoski, Jonathan Katz, Kalaiselvi Kamaraj

title: Optimize traffic costs of Amazon MSK consumers on Amazon EKS with rack awareness
key_points: Kafka consumers can read from a replica in their own Availability Zone, but pods on EKS do not know their zone; a Kyverno policy injects it so each pod sets the right rack id at start-up.
Cuts cross-zone data transfer charges for consumers of MSK topics; long, Kubernetes-heavy walkthrough.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon EKS, Kyverno
decision: Accept cross-AZ consumer traffic vs rack-aware consumers pinned to their zone's replica
authors: Austin Groeneveld, Farooq Ashraf

title: Automate data lineage in Amazon SageMaker using AWS Glue Crawlers supported data sources
key_points: When a Glue crawler catalogues S3 or DynamoDB sources, SageMaker Catalog can capture table- and column-level lineage automatically and show it as a graph.
The graph also tracks schema changes over time, which helps impact analysis before changing a pipeline step.
Mostly console setup inside Unified Studio.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, AWS Glue, Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
decision: Automatic catalog lineage from crawlers vs lineage from the transformation tool (e.g. dbt docs) for impact analysis
authors: Mohit Dawar, Jose Romero

title: Accelerate your data quality journey for lakehouse architecture with Amazon SageMaker, Apache Iceberg on AWS, Amazon S3 tables, and AWS Glue Data Quality
key_points: Glue Data Quality can now recommend and run rules on Iceberg tables in ordinary S3 buckets (under Lake Formation) and on S3 Tables, checking data at rest after it is written.
Glue jobs build both tables from NYC taxi data; the post then generates rule recommendations, runs them and shows the scores in SageMaker Unified Studio.
Direct follow-up to the reader's own data quality work: the same rule language, now on lakehouse tables.
services: AWS Glue Data Quality, AWS Glue, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
decision: Quality checks in the pipeline before publishing vs scheduled checks at rest on Iceberg / S3 Tables
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Data Quality Check (done) follow-up; lakehouse (later)
authors: Brody Pearman, Narayani Ambashta, Shiv Narayanan, Shriya Vanvari

title: Trusted identity propagation using IAM Identity Center for Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: OpenSearch UI can now pass the signed-in Identity Center user through to OpenSearch domains and collections, so access is decided per user and group without a SAML hop.
Fine-grained index and document rules map to Identity Center groups; search-side security only.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, AWS IAM Identity Center
authors: Muthu Pitchaimani, Sohaib Katariwala

title: Secure generative SQL with Amazon Q
key_points: Explains how Amazon Q generative SQL in Redshift Query Editor and Unified Studio builds prompts only from schema metadata the connected user can already see, caches it encrypted, and refreshes it periodically.
Accuracy levers: custom context with table and column descriptions, include/exclude rules for schemas and topics, and optional access to query history, which can expose other users' query text.
Covers cross-Region inference and CloudTrail monitoring; a security checklist more than a build.
services: Amazon Q, Amazon Redshift, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS KMS
decision: Schema-only context vs adding custom context and query history for text-to-SQL accuracy vs metadata exposure
authors: Gregory Knowles, Abhinav Tripathy, Erol Murtezaoglu

title: Optimize industrial IoT analytics with Amazon Data Firehose and Amazon S3 Tables with Apache Iceberg
key_points: Factory sensor readings go over MQTT to an IoT Greengrass edge gateway, which forwards them through Firehose into S3 Tables, ready to query in Athena.
Relies on S3 Tables' automatic maintenance instead of running compaction, and scales to more plants by adding gateways; low-code, little custom logic.
services: Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS IoT Greengrass, Amazon Athena
decision: Firehose straight into S3 Tables vs a stream plus processing engine for low-transform sensor ingestion
authors: Ashok Padmanabhan, Joyson Neville Lewis, Anil Vure

title: Build an analytics pipeline that is resilient to Avro schema changes using Amazon Athena
key_points: For Hive-style Avro tables partitioned by hour, the post keeps queries working through frequent schema changes by updating the Glue table's Avro schema literal through the API and using Athena partition projection.
A script detects a new schema in arriving files and triggers the table update, so old and new partitions stay readable under the latest schema.
Explicitly not for Iceberg, which handles schema evolution natively; mainly useful for legacy Hive tables.
services: Amazon Athena, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon S3, Apache Avro
decision: Hive tables with managed Avro schema literals vs moving to Iceberg for frequently changing source schemas
authors: Mohammad Sabeel, Indira Balakrishnan

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service 101: How many shards do I need
key_points: Beginner guide to sizing OpenSearch indexes: pick the primary shard count mainly from expected storage per shard, and do not fear a single shard for small indexes.
Search-cluster basics only.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Tom Burns, Ron Miller

title: Introducing MCP Server for Apache Spark History Server for AI-powered debugging and optimization
key_points: An open-source MCP server exposes Spark History Server data (applications, jobs, stages, tasks, SQL plans) so an AI assistant can explain why a run failed or slowed down instead of the engineer clicking through the Spark UI.
Read-only data layer that runs locally or on EC2/EKS and works with Glue and EMR event logs as well as self-managed Spark.
The managed Spark optimization agent covered in Nov 2026 builds on the same idea, so this is mostly background.
services: Apache Spark, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, Model Context Protocol
decision: Manual Spark UI analysis vs AI-assisted diagnosis over Spark History Server data for slow or failed Glue jobs
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Redshift ETL failure alert (planned); cost optimization (later)
authors: Manabu McCloskey, Andrew Kim, Mohit Saxena, Kartik Panjabi, Shubham Mehta, Vara Bonthu

title: Workload management in OpenSearch-based multi-tenant centralized logging platforms
key_points: For a shared logging cluster, tenants are tiered and placed by importance, a rules-based proxy throttles or reroutes heavy requests, and OpenSearch workload groups cap each tenant's search resources.
Walks through a security incident and a month-end reporting spike; relevant only to teams running logging on OpenSearch.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Ezat Karimi, Jon Handler

title: Improve RabbitMQ performance on Amazon MQ with AWS Graviton3-based M7g instances
key_points: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ can now run on Graviton3-based brokers, with smaller disk sizes for clusters.
AWS reports up to 50% more workload capacity and up to 85% more throughput than comparable previous-generation brokers; instance launch note only.
services: Amazon MQ, AWS Graviton
authors: Vignesh Selvam, Vinodh Kannan Sadayamuthu, Samuel Massé

title: Accelerating development with the AWS Data Processing MCP Server and Agent
key_points: An open-source MCP server lets an AI assistant read and act on Glue jobs and crawlers, the Data Catalog, Athena and EMR in the reader's own account, with write actions behind an explicit flag.
Example flows: onboard a CSV end to end (S3, crawler, table, Athena workgroup), turn a business question into joined SQL, and summarise Glue job or EMR cluster health and cost.
Also released as a stand-alone Strands agent; access is scoped by the IAM role it runs under, which is the main design point to explain.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Model Context Protocol, Strands Agents
decision: Console and CLI by hand vs an AI assistant with read-only vs write access to the data platform through MCP
attaches_to: aws-bytes: GenAI on data (later); dbt-pipelines (Athena folder)
authors: Shubham Mehta, Arun A K, Liyuan Lin, Mohit Saxena, Vaibhav Naik, Pradeep Patel, Sarath Krishnan

title: Optimizing vector search using Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Two preview integrations: OpenSearch managed clusters can keep vectors in S3 Vectors for cheaper, slower storage, and an S3 vector index can be exported to OpenSearch Serverless when fast search is needed.
The idea is tiering embeddings by how often they are queried; vector-search territory, off the reader's path.
services: Amazon S3 Vectors, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
authors: Sohaib Katariwala, Bobby Mohammed, Sorabh Hamirwasia, Mark Twomey, Pallavi Priyadarshini

title: Unifying data insights with AWS Quick Sight and Amazon SageMaker
key_points: A Unified Studio project can open a catalog asset straight in Quick Sight, and the resulting dashboards are published back to the catalog as searchable, shareable assets.
BI-tool integration walkthrough with no data engineering content.
services: Amazon Quick Sight, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Catalog
authors: Ramon Lopez, Leonardo Gomez

title: Scale your AWS Glue for Apache Spark jobs with R type, G.12X, and G.16X workers
key_points: Glue adds memory-heavy R workers (more memory per vCPU than G workers) and two larger G sizes, so a job can scale up per worker rather than only out.
Lists where adding workers does not help: broadcast and skewed joins, high-cardinality group-bys, big windows, large query plans on the driver, heavy caching.
Worked example: a skewed job fails on G workers with executors out of space and memory, then completes on R workers of the same DPU size; easy to reproduce on a small skewed dataset.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Spark
decision: More standard workers vs larger G workers vs memory-optimised R workers (vs fixing the skew) for memory-bound Glue jobs
authors: Noritaka Sekiyama, Matt Su, Sean McGeehan, Tomohiro Tanaka, Peter Tsai

title: Integrating Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion with Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora
key_points: OpenSearch Ingestion can now keep a search index in sync with Aurora or RDS (MySQL and PostgreSQL): an initial snapshot export, then ongoing changes read from the database's replication log.
Replaces custom sync jobs for adding full-text and faceted search to a transactional database; a search use case, not analytics.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Aurora, Amazon RDS
authors: Michael Torio, Arjun Nambiar, Sohaib Katariwala

title: Unifying metadata governance across Amazon SageMaker and Collibra
key_points: A CloudFormation-deployed sync job copies asset metadata from SageMaker Catalog into Collibra, and Collibra workflows drive subscription approvals back in SageMaker.
Only relevant to organisations already standardised on Collibra.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, Collibra, AWS Lambda
authors: Collibra — Vasiliki Nikolopoulou, Divij Bhatia, Leonardo Gomez

title: Revenue NSW modernises analytics with AWS, enabling unified and scalable data management, processing, and access
key_points: A state revenue agency replaced end-of-life on-premises analytics hardware with Redshift as the single source of truth, chosen after a PoC on completeness, speed and total cost.
Ingestion uses one pattern per source type: DMS for full load plus ongoing CDC from Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server; AppFlow for Salesforce; event-triggered Glue jobs for hundreds of partner files.
AWS reports PoC queries typically ran 5 to 50 times faster than on premises; short story with no build detail.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS Database Migration Service, AWS Glue, Amazon AppFlow, Amazon S3
decision: One ingestion pattern per source type (DMS CDC vs SaaS connector vs event-driven Glue) feeding a single Redshift warehouse
attaches_to: aws-bytes: change data capture - DMS vs zero-ETL (later)
authors: Revenue NSW — Saeed Barghi, Moha Alsouli, Miroslaw (Mick) Mioduszewski

title: Orchestrate data processing jobs, querybooks, and notebooks using visual workflow experience in Amazon SageMaker
key_points: A drag-and-drop workflow builder in SageMaker Unified Studio chains a job, a SQL querybook and a notebook, and generates the Airflow DAG behind the scenes.
Early launch tutorial; later posts on SageMaker workflows and MWAA Serverless cover the orchestration choice in more depth.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon MWAA
authors: Naohisa Takahashi, Regan Perk, Gal Heyne, Yuhang Huang, Iris Tian, Noritaka Sekiyama

title: Introducing Jobs in Amazon SageMaker
key_points: SageMaker Unified Studio gets a jobs page for Glue-style data processing jobs built from code, notebooks or the visual editor, with scheduling, run history and AI-assisted error analysis.
A console experience on top of Glue; nothing beyond running Glue jobs directly.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Glue
authors: Chiho Sugimoto, Matt Su, Noritaka Sekiyama

title: Compaction support for Avro and ORC file formats in Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon S3
key_points: Automatic compaction in S3 Tables and in Glue Data Catalog optimisation now covers Iceberg tables stored as Avro or ORC, not only Parquet.

Benchmark streams simulated IoT data from MSK through EMR Serverless into compacted and uncompacted tables, then compares Athena query times; AWS reports gains in the range of roughly 12% to 40% per query.
Includes a handy Parquet vs ORC vs Avro comparison; the gains are modest because the writer already produced large files.
services: Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon EMR Serverless, Amazon MSK, Amazon Athena
decision: Parquet vs ORC vs Avro as the Iceberg file format, and managed vs no compaction for streaming-written tables
authors: Angel Conde Manjon, Diego Colombatto, Sandeep Adwankar

title: Harnessing the Power of Nested Materialized Views and exploring Cascading Refresh
key_points: Redshift materialized views can be built on other materialized views, so a join shared by several dashboards is computed once and extended layer by layer.
A cascading refresh brings the whole chain up to date in one command, in dependency order.
Introductory; the Nov 2026 materialized-views deep dive covers refresh behaviour and tuning more fully, so this is background for that write-up.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift materialized views
decision: Nested materialized views with cascading refresh vs separate pipeline steps vs dbt table models for layered BI aggregates
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (dbt materialized_view models on Redshift Serverless)
authors: Ritesh Sinha, Raza Hafeez, Ricardo Serafim

title: Realizing ocean data democratization: Furuno Electric’s initiatives using Amazon DataZone
key_points: Furuno replaced per-project data stacks with one CDK-built platform that stamps out a standard ingestion pipeline (IoT Core, Kinesis, Lambda, Glue, S3) for each new product.
Control Tower sets the security baseline across accounts, and DataZone handles discovery and sharing, with Glue Data Quality owned by a dedicated data management team.
Much of the post is about organisation design: separate platform and data teams under a chief data officer.
services: Amazon DataZone, AWS Glue, AWS Glue Data Quality, AWS Control Tower, Amazon Kinesis, AWS CDK
decision: Per-project data stacks vs one templated shared platform with central governance
authors: Furuno Electric — Akira Mikami, Mitsuhiko Nishida, Junpei Ozono

title: Geospatial data lakes with Amazon Redshift
key_points: A CSV of clinic locations is crawled into the Glue catalog, secured with Lake Formation tags so GIS analysts see only non-sensitive columns, and queried from Redshift Serverless.
Redshift's GEOMETRY type and spatial functions turn the lake data into points inside a view, which ArcGIS Pro reads directly as a map layer.
Niche use case, but a clean example of column-level lake security enforced on Redshift Spectrum queries.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS Lake Formation, AWS Glue, Amazon S3, AWS CloudFormation
decision: Keep geospatial data in the lake behind Lake Formation vs load it into Redshift tables for GIS tools
authors: Jeremy Spell, Jeff DeMuth

title: Perform per-project cost allocation in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: SageMaker Unified Studio tags the resources it provisions with domain and project identifiers; activating those as cost allocation tags lets finance split the bill per project.
Shows the result in Cost Explorer and in a Data Exports plus Quick Sight dashboard; only relevant once teams actually work inside Unified Studio.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Data Exports, Amazon Quick Sight
authors: Enrique Salgado Hernández, Angel Conde Manjon

title: Develop and monitor a Spark application using existing data in Amazon S3 with Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: Console walkthrough: attach EMR Serverless as compute in a SageMaker Unified Studio project, develop a Spark job in a notebook over existing S3 data, and inspect it in the Spark UI.
Scheduling goes through MWAA; introductory platform tour with no design trade-off.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon EMR Serverless, Amazon MWAA, Amazon S3
authors: Amit Maindola, Abhilash Nagilla

title: Near real-time baggage operational insights for airlines using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: IBM's reference design splits an airline's monolithic baggage database into DynamoDB tables per business capability and streams changes out for near real-time analytics instead of nightly batch loads.
Explains why Kinesis Data Streams was chosen over DynamoDB Streams for the change feed: fan-out to several consumers, longer retention for replay, and direct Flink integration.
Flink does windowed aggregation and anomaly detection before results land in Aurora or DynamoDB for reporting; high level, no build steps.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon Aurora, AWS Glue, Amazon Quick Sight
decision: DynamoDB Streams vs Kinesis Data Streams for change capture from an operational DynamoDB store with several downstream consumers
attaches_to: aws-bytes: real-time streaming / change data capture (later)
authors: IBM — Subhash Sharma, Neeraj Kaushik, Jay Pandya, Vijay Gokarn

title: Overcome your Kafka Connect challenges with Amazon Data Firehose
key_points: Firehose can now start reading an MSK topic from the earliest offset or a chosen timestamp, not only from the moment the stream was created.
That removes the stop-drain-restart dance when replacing self-run Kafka Connect S3 sink connectors with Firehose, and lets a first-time sink backfill the topic's history.
Mostly feature walkthrough; the Nov 2026 post on delivering Kafka data to S3 covers the cost side of the same choice.
services: Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon MSK, Amazon S3, Kafka Connect
decision: Self-managed Kafka Connect sink vs Firehose for delivering MSK topics to S3
authors: Swapna Bandla, Austin Groeneveld

title: How Stifel built a modern data platform using AWS Glue and an event-driven domain architecture
key_points: Stifel runs a data mesh where each business domain builds its own data products on Glue jobs over Hudi tables, shared through a central Lake Formation governance account.
Ingestion is metadata-driven: file arrivals are logged by Lambda into an Aurora PostgreSQL audit store, and Step Functions batches unprocessed files into parallel Glue jobs with quality checks.

The reusable idea is refresh by event rather than by schedule: producers emit a refresh event to a central EventBridge bus, and consumers start their own pipelines only once all upstream dependencies have reported in.
services: AWS Glue, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Apache Hudi, Amazon Athena
aws_type: Best Practices / Experience-Based Acceleration / Technical How-to / Thought Leadership · 300
decision: Fixed batch schedules vs event-driven, dependency-aware refresh for data products shared across domains
authors: Stifel — Amit Maindola, Srinivas Kandi, Hossein Johari, Ahmad Rawashdeh, Lei Meng

title: Kaltura reduces observability operational costs by 60% with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Kaltura replaced a SaaS logging product with OpenSearch Service fed by OpenSearch Ingestion, adding role-based access per team and trace-to-log correlation.
AWS reports about 60% lower cost with longer log retention; an observability-platform story away from the data engineering path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion
authors: Kaltura — Ido Ziv, Roi Gamliel, Yonatan Dolan

title: Enhance stability with dedicated cluster manager nodes using Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Explains why production OpenSearch domains should separate cluster-management duties from data nodes, and how to choose the count and instance size of dedicated manager nodes.
Cluster-operations advice for search teams only.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Chinmayi Narasimhadevara, Imtiaz Sayed

title: Build conversational AI search with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Builds a RAG chatbot inside OpenSearch: a Bedrock model connector, an ingest pipeline that embeds documents, and an OpenSearch agent that keeps conversation memory for follow-up questions.
Search-side GenAI build; nothing about data pipelines or warehousing.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Bedrock
authors: Bharav Patel

title: Introducing GenAI-powered business description recommendations for custom assets in Amazon SageMaker Catalog
key_points: SageMaker Catalog can now draft table summaries, use cases and column descriptions with an LLM for assets registered through the API, such as Iceberg tables or third-party datasets.
Stewards review and edit the suggestions before publishing; a short console walkthrough with no design trade-off.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, Amazon Bedrock
authors: Ramesh H Singh, Balaji Kumar Gopalakrishnan, Mark Horta, Mohit Dawar, Pradeep Misra
